stem: A 42-year-old man presents to your emergency department 6 hours after his GP started tramadol 100 mg three times daily for back pain. He has been on sertraline 100 mg daily for 3 years for depression. On arrival he is agitated, sweating and tremulous. Examination shows a rigid trunk but rhythmic lower limb clonus that is more prominent than upper. His temperature is 38.9 C and he is tachycardic. Pupils are widely dilated with brisk hyperreflexia in the lower limbs.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 168/98, RR 22, SpO2 98 percent, temp 38.9 C
data_table.Examination: Agitated, sweaty, tremulous; dilated pupils; lower limb rhythmic clonus > upper; hyperreflexia lower limbs; rigid trunk but not lead-pipe; alert and orientated
data_table.Investigations: CK 250 U/L (<200), Na 138 mmol/L, K 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, VBG pH 7.35

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease sertraline and tramadol, IV fluid resuscitation, IV diazepam 5 to 10 mg titrated for agitation and hyperthermia, active cooling and admit for observation with a target temperature under 38 C
options.rationale: Rapid onset serotonergic clinical triad (autonomic instability, neuromuscular excitation with clonus, altered mental state) after adding tramadol to sertraline is serotonin syndrome; management is withdrawal, benzodiazepines, cooling and supportive care.
source_refs: AMH: Serotonin syndrome and NMS discrimination

options.text: IV bromocriptine 2.5 mg orally 8 hourly plus IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg loading dose treating neuroleptic malignant syndrome then transfer to intensive care for continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: NMS has bradykinesia, lead-pipe rigidity throughout, more gradual onset over days on dopamine antagonists and is associated with markedly raised CK, not lower limb clonus and hyperreflexia within hours.
source_refs: AMH: Serotonin syndrome and NMS discrimination

options.text: Continue current medications, start IV paracetamol 1 g and IV metoclopramide 10 mg to control fever and nausea, observation for 6 hours to see if the symptoms settle spontaneously today
options.rationale: Continuing offending drugs perpetuates serotonergic toxicity; metoclopramide has additional prokinetic and dopamine antagonist effects and paracetamol does not treat serotonin syndrome.

options.text: IV haloperidol 5 mg for agitation and IV droperidol 10 mg for hyperthermia while continuing tramadol for analgesia and sertraline for underlying depressed mood over the acute presentation window
options.rationale: Antipsychotics may worsen autonomic instability, extrapyramidal features and hyperthermia in serotonin syndrome; benzodiazepines are the AU first-line sedative.

options.text: IV physostigmine 1 mg to reverse anticholinergic delirium and IV lorazepam 2 mg for the tremor while awaiting return of the initial drug screen results to guide further management this evening
options.rationale: This is not anticholinergic toxidrome; physostigmine is not indicated. The clinical picture is serotonergic and management is different.
source_refs: AMH: Serotonin syndrome and NMS discrimination

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome presents rapidly (within 24 hours) after a serotonergic drug interaction with a triad of autonomic instability, neuromuscular excitation (lower limb-predominant clonus, hyperreflexia) and altered mental state. NMS has a gradual onset over days on dopamine antagonists with lead-pipe rigidity throughout, marked CK elevation, bradyreflexia and less clonus. Management of serotonin syndrome: withdraw offending drugs, IV benzodiazepines for sedation and rigidity, cooling and supportive care; cyproheptadine is second-line for refractory cases.
key_points: Rapid onset after drug interaction with clonus > rigidity = serotonin syndrome
Withdraw offending drugs and treat with benzodiazepines
Lower limb clonus more than upper is characteristic
NMS: slower onset, lead-pipe rigidity, high CK, dopamine antagonist
explanation.pearls: Cyproheptadine 12 mg orally then 2 mg every 2 hours as needed is a serotonin-2A antagonist used in refractory serotonin syndrome under Poisons Information advice; it is not first-line but reserved for severe cases not settling with benzodiazepines.

sources.label: AMH: Serotonin syndrome and NMS discrimination

stem: A 24-year-old woman with a documented diagnosis of borderline personality disorder is brought to your emergency department by her mother at 2 am after cutting her forearms superficially with a broken glass. This is her 8th presentation in 6 months. Her mother reports she was upset after a fight with her boyfriend. On arrival she is tearful but co-operative and denies suicidal intent. Wounds are shallow, non-bleeding and require 3 stitches. She has no acute medical concerns.

data_table.Examination: Multiple superficial linear lacerations left forearm, shallow bleeding stopped; older well-healed scars right forearm; calm engagement, tearful, orientated; no acute intoxication signs
data_table.Investigations: Not otherwise indicated; BAC 0.02 percent; UDS negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Admit for a minimum 72 hour psychiatric observation on the acute unit for containment given repeat presentations, prescribe olanzapine 5 mg orally at night and defer any outpatient follow-up planning until after discharge
options.rationale: Prolonged admission and antipsychotic prescription for BPD self-harm typically worsens outcomes by regression and dependence; RANZCP advises minimising admission and connecting to outpatient care.

options.text: Refer to the on-call psychiatric registrar for consideration of involuntary admission under the Mental Health Act for ongoing suicide risk given the recurrent nature of these episodic presentations
options.rationale: There is no active suicidal intent and no acute mental illness requiring involuntary treatment; BPD self-harm does not itself meet criteria under most AU MHAs.

options.text: Discharge with paracetamol advice and no formal psychiatric follow-up as she has an established BPD diagnosis and outpatient team, provide a brief written summary to her general practitioner in the morning
options.rationale: Discharge without connection to outpatient team or crisis plan misses opportunity to reinforce skills use and continuity of care; AU guidelines advise active follow-up within 48 hours.

options.text: Attend to the wounds, calmly discuss the trigger with a validating approach, agree a short crisis plan with her outpatient team including safety planning and dialectical behaviour therapy, arrange follow-up within 48 hours
options.rationale: AU RANZCP BPD clinical practice guideline emphasises validation, containment, crisis planning and rapid connection to outpatient treatment (ideally DBT), avoiding hospitalisation which can reinforce dependence and iatrogenic harm.

options.text: Prescribe short course quetiapine 25 mg orally three times daily for 2 weeks to manage emotional dysregulation, provide GP letter and discharge without psychiatric team review while she is asymptomatic
options.rationale: Routine quetiapine or other antipsychotic for BPD emotional dysregulation is not evidence-based first-line; sedative use in a crisis often reinforces coping avoidance and confers side effects.

explanation.summary: AU RANZCP borderline personality disorder guidelines recommend a structured, validating, non-hospitalising approach to self-harm presentations with a short-stay assessment, treatment of wounds, agreed crisis plan, rapid outpatient follow-up (ideally with a DBT or MBT programme) and avoidance of routine admission or off-label antipsychotic prescribing. Involuntary treatment is reserved for acute mental illness or genuine imminent risk to life.
key_points: Validation, containment and crisis planning first
Rapid outpatient follow-up within 48 hours (DBT or MBT)
Avoid routine admission or antipsychotic prescription for BPD self-harm
Involuntary treatment only for co-morbid mental illness or imminent risk
explanation.pearls: The Australian NHMRC BPD guideline specifies that no medication is approved for the core features of BPD in Australia; short-term medication targeting acute co-morbid symptoms (SSRIs for depression, second-generation antipsychotics for transient psychotic features) is used only with regular review and clear stop criteria.

stem: A 37-year-old woman with bipolar disorder is admitted to your acute psychiatry unit after 5 days of increasing withdrawal, mutism and refusal to eat or drink. On examination she sits motionless on the edge of the bed, mute, staring, does not respond to verbal command but resists passive movement of her limbs. She holds her right arm in the air after you place it there. She has no fever. Recent medications include lithium and olanzapine 20 mg. Bloods including CK, TFT and calcium are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 68, BP 110/72, RR 12, SpO2 98 percent, temp 36.5 C
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, gaze fixed; waxy flexibility on limb positioning; posturing sustained 60 seconds; negativism resisting passive movement; grimacing; no lead-pipe rigidity; no autonomic instability
data_table.Investigations: CK 180 U/L (<200), Na 138 mmol/L, TSH 2.4 mIU/L, calcium 2.35 mmol/L; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic and initial management step?

options.text: IV haloperidol 5 mg intramuscularly for control of the acute agitation and psychotic symptoms and IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg loading dose for the accompanying rigidity while transferring to intensive care
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and precipitate NMS; there is no autonomic instability or high CK to indicate NMS or dantrolene.

options.text: IV lorazepam 2 mg bolus with observation of catatonia scale response over 15 minutes, aiming for at least 50 percent Bush-Francis reduction, and repeat dosing 6-hourly if partial response
options.rationale: The presentation meets Bush-Francis catatonia criteria (mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, posturing, negativism); the lorazepam challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic in AU practice.

options.text: Commence sodium valproate 500 mg orally twice daily and IV normal saline 1000 mL over 4 hours for supportive dehydration management pending psychiatric team review in the morning ward round
options.rationale: Valproate does not treat catatonia acutely; the AU standard is a lorazepam challenge given the same day, not deferring to a morning review.

options.text: Continue olanzapine, add sertraline 50 mg orally daily for underlying mood, IV normal saline 1000 mL over 4 hours and observe for 48 hours in the acute unit for spontaneous response
options.rationale: Continuing olanzapine may perpetuate catatonia; SSRI addition does not treat catatonia and delays effective diagnostic-therapeutic lorazepam trial.

options.text: Refer for ECT the following morning without a lorazepam challenge as ECT is the definitive treatment for catatonia and delaying with a benzodiazepine trial adds no additional diagnostic information
options.rationale: Lorazepam challenge precedes ECT because it is faster, safer, less resource-intensive and diagnostically important; ECT is used when lorazepam fails or is contraindicated.

explanation.summary: Catatonia is recognised on the Bush-Francis scale requiring three or more of mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, negativism, posturing, echolalia, echopraxia and stereotypies. The lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV, expecting at least 50 percent reduction in Bush-Francis score within 15 to 30 minutes) is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Antipsychotics are held or reduced because they can worsen catatonia. ECT is reserved for lorazepam-refractory or life-threatening catatonia.
key_points: Bush-Francis criteria: 3 or more of mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, posturing, negativism
Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic
Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia; hold or reduce them
ECT for lorazepam-refractory or malignant catatonia
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability, rigidity, altered consciousness) has high mortality and requires immediate ECT if lorazepam fails; distinguish clinically from neuroleptic malignant syndrome by the presence of catatonic features preceding antipsychotic exposure or persisting despite antipsychotic withdrawal.

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD diagnosis and driving obligations
stem: A 30-year-old primary school teacher attends your GP clinic asking for assessment for possible attention deficit hyperactivity disorder after her nephew was diagnosed. She reports lifelong difficulty finishing tasks, chronic time blindness, poor sleep because her mind races, and multiple career changes. Her school reports at age 8 mention she is bright but does not finish her work. She drives daily including for work, has no seizures, no substance use and is otherwise well. She scores 17/24 on the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale.

data_table.Examination: Alert, engaging, mild psychomotor restlessness; euthymic; no cognitive deficit at bedside; no dysmorphism
data_table.Investigations: TSH 2.1 mIU/L, iron studies within normal limits, FBC and UEC within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence dexamphetamine 5 mg orally twice daily as a therapeutic trial and review clinical response in 4 weeks in general practice before deciding on formal specialist referral for the ADHD assessment
options.rationale: GPs cannot legally initiate stimulants for ADHD in most AU jurisdictions; assessment and initiation are a specialist role in state authority framework.

options.text: Reassure that the ASRS is only a screening tool with limited specificity, provide sleep hygiene advice and refer for CBT for adult inattention symptoms while deferring any formal diagnostic assessment for 6 months
options.rationale: ASRS positive plus functional impairment and lifelong symptoms warrants specialist assessment; deferring 6 months without addressing established impairment is not the AU pathway.
source_refs: RANZCP Adult ADHD clinical practice guideline

options.text: Advise her to stop driving immediately pending diagnostic assessment and treatment initiation as untreated adult ADHD is deemed to preclude a safe class C car licence under Austroads standards
options.rationale: AU Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive does not automatically preclude driving for untreated ADHD; a fitness assessment applies only where symptoms create demonstrated risk.

options.text: Order neuropsychological testing including Wisconsin Card Sort and Trail Making tests in general practice to formally diagnose ADHD before making any specialist referral or considering any treatment options
options.rationale: Neuropsychological testing supplements clinical diagnosis but is not the diagnostic gateway; specialist psychiatric interview with collateral history is the primary AU standard.

options.text: Refer to a psychiatrist or specialist paediatric-adult ADHD service for structured diagnostic assessment including collateral childhood history, comorbidity screen and consideration of stimulant treatment
options.rationale: AU RANZCP practice guideline requires specialist psychiatrist assessment (or dual-trained paediatrician) for adult ADHD diagnosis including collateral history and comorbidity screen before stimulants are initiated.
source_refs: RANZCP Adult ADHD clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: AU adult ADHD assessment requires specialist psychiatrist review with a structured diagnostic interview, collateral childhood history (school reports, family members), functional impairment across two settings, comorbidity screen and exclusion of alternative causes. Stimulant treatment is initiated by an authorised specialist under state authority. Driving is generally permitted unless active impairment is demonstrated; patients on stimulants should be counselled to declare medications on licence review as per Austroads standards.
key_points: Adult ADHD diagnosis is specialist psychiatrist (or dual paediatrician) responsibility
Collateral childhood history required for diagnosis
Stimulant initiation requires state authority
Driving allowed unless demonstrated impairment (Austroads)
explanation.pearls: Untreated adult ADHD is associated with increased motor vehicle crash risk in cohort studies; stimulant treatment reduces this risk, so document a clear pre and post treatment driving history and encourage patients to consider medication effect on driving performance when planning long or high-risk driving.

sources.label: RANZCP Adult ADHD clinical practice guideline

stem: A 52-year-old woman is referred to your community mental health team by her GP because for 18 months she has been convinced her neighbour is releasing carbon monoxide gas through her bedroom wall to poison her. She has had the vents boarded up and installed multiple detectors that consistently read zero. She works full-time as a bookkeeper without difficulty, maintains social contact with three long-term friends, and reports no hallucinations. Her mood is euthymic. On mental state she is well-groomed, articulate and no formal thought disorder. Cognitive screen is normal.

data_table.Examination: Well-groomed, articulate; euthymic; no formal thought disorder; single persistent non-bizarre delusion regarding neighbour poisoning; no hallucinations; insight absent regarding delusion, preserved regarding functioning; MMSE 30/30
data_table.Investigations: TSH 2.4 mIU/L, B12 320 pmol/L, folate within normal limits, CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and initial pharmacological approach?

options.text: Schizophrenia paranoid subtype; olanzapine 10 mg orally at night with community mental health team weekly follow-up, weight and metabolic monitoring at baseline, 6 weeks and 3 months
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires 6 months of prodromal or active phase symptoms including hallucinations, negative symptoms or disorganisation; preserved functioning and single non-bizarre delusion fits delusional disorder.

options.text: Late-onset psychosis secondary to dementia; commence donepezil 5 mg orally daily and refer to memory clinic for MRI, formal neuropsychology and progressive cognitive care planning for the household
options.rationale: Normal cognitive screen and preserved functioning make dementia unlikely; donepezil does not treat isolated delusional disorder.

options.text: Delusional disorder (persecutory type); slow low-dose risperidone 0.5 mg orally at night titrated over 6 weeks with regular RANZCP outcome measure review and engagement in trust-building therapy
options.rationale: A single non-bizarre delusion for over one month with preserved functioning, no hallucinations and no thought disorder meets DSM-5-TR delusional disorder criteria; low-dose antipsychotic with slow titration and therapeutic engagement is standard.

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder; monitor without antipsychotic for 4 weeks awaiting spontaneous resolution, review in 4 weeks with the community mental health team before any pharmacological intervention
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder is under 1 month duration; 18 months excludes this diagnosis.

options.text: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features; sertraline 100 mg orally daily plus low-dose olanzapine 5 mg orally at night as combination pharmacotherapy for mood-congruent psychotic symptoms
options.rationale: Depressive psychosis requires prominent mood symptoms; she is euthymic and there is no depressive syndrome.

explanation.summary: Delusional disorder is diagnosed when a persistent non-bizarre delusion (persecutory, jealous, erotomanic, grandiose or somatic) is present for at least one month, functioning is not markedly impaired outside the delusion, no hallucinations are prominent, and criteria for schizophrenia are not met. Treatment is low-dose antipsychotic (risperidone or olanzapine) with slow titration, plus supportive engagement acknowledging the patient's distress without endorsing the delusion. Insight and treatment adherence are often poor, so slow trust-building is central.
key_points: Delusional disorder = non-bizarre delusion >=1 month, preserved function
No prominent hallucinations, no thought disorder
Low-dose antipsychotic (risperidone) with slow titration
Trust-building engagement without endorsing or challenging delusion directly
explanation.pearls: Response rates in delusional disorder are lower than schizophrenia and require patience with slow titration and long trials; folie a deux (shared delusional disorder) may develop in close contacts who withdraw from the shared belief on separation from the primary case.

stem: A 34-year-old woman migrated from Vietnam 6 months ago and attends your general practice for routine health assessment. She is well with no cough, no fever, no weight loss and no night sweats. She has never been treated for tuberculosis but recalls a household contact with active TB when she was 15. She is HIV negative and not immunosuppressed. Chest X-ray is clear. Her QFT-Plus is positive. She wishes to have children within 12 months.

data_table.Examination: Systemically well; clear chest on auscultation; no lymphadenopathy; no skin findings
data_table.Investigations: QFT-Plus positive; chest X-ray no active disease; HIV negative; HBV/HCV negative; LFTs within normal limits; not pregnant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment offer?

options.text: Rifampicin 600 mg orally daily plus isoniazid 300 mg orally daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg orally daily for 3 months (3HR) with monthly LFT and hepatitis symptom review during treatment
options.rationale: AU CDNA and TSANZ latent TB treatment recommends 3HR (3 month rifampicin plus isoniazid) as preferred regimen due to shorter duration, better completion and equal efficacy to 6H; pyridoxine prevents peripheral neuropathy.

options.text: Isoniazid 300 mg orally daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg orally daily for 9 months (9H) as this remains the AU first-line regimen for latent TB in adults with normal baseline liver function
options.rationale: 9H is a legacy regimen; AU has moved to shorter regimens (3HR or 4R) as first-line to improve completion rates.

options.text: Rifampicin 600 mg orally daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg orally daily monotherapy for 4 months (4R) with monthly LFT monitoring and screening for drug interactions including hormonal contraception
options.rationale: 4R is an accepted alternative if isoniazid contraindicated; when both agents can be given, 3HR is preferred as shorter than 4R in AU pathways.

options.text: No treatment as latent TB is asymptomatic and treatment risk outweighs benefit in a low-transmission country like Australia, provide symptom checklist and annual review in general practice
options.rationale: Recent migration from a high-incidence country and known household contact confer a lifetime reactivation risk of 5 to 10 percent; treatment materially reduces this and is offered per AU guidance.

options.text: Repeat QFT-Plus in 6 months to confirm the positive result before commencing any treatment, as isolated QFT-Plus positivity has a false positive rate that warrants a repeat test for diagnostic certainty
options.rationale: In a person with known past exposure, single QFT-Plus positive is sufficient for LTBI diagnosis; repeat delays treatment without changing management.

explanation.summary: Latent tuberculosis infection in a person from a high-incidence country with a positive interferon-gamma release assay, clear chest X-ray and no symptoms warrants offered treatment to prevent reactivation. AU preferred regimens are 3HR (rifampicin plus isoniazid for 3 months) or 4R (rifampicin monotherapy for 4 months), with pyridoxine to prevent isoniazid neuropathy. Monthly LFT monitoring and hepatitis symptom review during treatment are standard. 9H is a legacy regimen with lower completion rates.
key_points: Positive QFT-Plus with clear XR and no symptoms = LTBI
3HR is AU preferred regimen (or 4R if isoniazid contraindicated)
Pyridoxine prevents INH peripheral neuropathy
Monthly LFTs and hepatitis symptom check during treatment
explanation.pearls: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4 and reduces efficacy of combined hormonal contraception, warfarin and many antiretrovirals; alternative contraception (copper IUD, DMPA) is planned before starting a rifampicin-containing regimen in women of reproductive age.
